anchors.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
anchors.quantity_described: Per-input/per-circuit compensation: ablating one attention layer causes another layer to compensate (Hydra effect), plus a counterbalancing late-MLP downregulation effect; not a per-checkpoint scalar.
anchors.verbatim_abstract_sentence: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token.

anchors.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
anchors.venue_year: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st ICML, PMLR 235:42836-42855); arXiv v1 23 Feb 2024, v2 26 May 2024
anchors.quantity_described: Per-head, per-prompt self-repair magnitude across several model families/sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution; attributes mechanisms (LayerNorm scaling, Anti-Erasure neurons) but does not scalarise self-repair into a single per-checkpoint model score.
anchors.verbatim_abstract_sentence: We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect).

anchors.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
anchors.quantity_described: Backup name-mover heads identified as part of a 26-head, 7-class circuit explanation for one task (IOI) in one model (GPT-2 small); a circuit description, not a checkpoint-comparable scalar.
anchors.verbatim_abstract_sentence: In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI).

scalarisation_hits.paper: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
scalarisation_hits.title: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
scalarisation_hits.quantity_described: CoAx: a label-free score per unit (attention head/component) measuring how much that unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set of components has been removed (conditional/second-order ablation growth), used to recover backup heads and score components for pruning; evaluated per-circuit via ROC-AUC against known backup-head ground truth (GPT-2-small IOI) and transferred to induction across eight models. Confirmed (via forward-citation sweep on BOTH anchors, see citation_sweep below) to be the only paper citing either self-repair anchor that turns self-repair/backup behaviour into any kind of quantitative score.
scalarisation_hits.behaviour_named: backup-head recovery / capability knockout / structured pruning (general mechanistic interpretability, not safety refusal)
scalarisation_hits.quote: We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed.

citation_sweep.overall_conclusion: Across the full forward-citation sets of both self-repair anchors (100 citing papers for Hydra Effect, capped by API limit; 36 citing papers for Rushing & Nanda, uncapped), the ONLY work found that turns self-repair/backup behaviour into any kind of quantitative score is Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx, arXiv:2607.01940), and it remains a per-unit/per-circuit score (ROC-AUC evaluated against backup-head ground truth within one model/circuit at a time), never reduced to one number per checkpoint used to compare or rank models. No new scalarisation candidate was found beyond the one already on record from the general web-search sweep.

W4.rationale: The full forward-citation sweep on both anchors (Semantic Scholar Graph API, 100+36=136 citing papers scanned with 5 distinct regex passes across the two anchors) is now complete and confirms no work reduces self-repair/backup behaviour to a per-checkpoint scalar used to compare, rank, or score model checkpoints. The two retried query families ('compensation coefficient ablation transformer layers' and 'how much of an ablated component is written back downstream') also returned zero relevant hits, backed by a positive control ('hydra effect language model self-repair', re-run in the same session, correctly surfaced the real McGrath et al. paper at position 1 of 10 -- proving the search backend was functioning and the other two queries' irrelevant results are true negatives, not backend failure). The nearest-neighbour paper (CoAx, arXiv:2607.01940) was tested with a zero-match regex for checkpoint/cross-checkpoint framing (0/140365 chars) with a working positive control on the same URL in the same session (143 matches for 'ablation'). The OPEN bar (>=3 distinct query families with zero relevant hits, AND >=1 positive-control-backed zero-match regex on the nearest-neighbour paper) is now met with margin: distinct zero-relevant-hit families are (1) 'backup heads redundancy transformer circuit', (2) 'self-repair across models comparison', (3) 'self-repair metric checkpoint', (4) 'compensation coefficient ablation transformer layers', (5) 'how much of an ablated component is written back downstream', (6) 'anti-erasure/negative head self-repair' (1 low-quality non-scalarising hit), plus (7) the citation sweep itself as an independent, exhaustive-within-both-anchors check. No CLOSED-worthy source was found in any of these, so the verdict does not soften to PARTIAL and does not upgrade to CLOSED -- it holds at OPEN.
